newsitem.title: UK: Investors irked as Gazprom issue price talked up.
newsitem.headline: Investors irked as Gazprom issue price talked up.

text.p: The opportunity to own a share of the world's largest natural gas company, Russia's RAO Gazprom, has captured the imagination of foreign investors, but talking up the issue price is putting people off.
"Investors are looking at the aftermarket and saying that talk of two dollars per share is fine, but if I wait a week I might be able to buy it at $1.20," said one London banker.
Talk on pricing for Russia's largest international share offer started at $1.25, then ratcheted rapidly higher through $1.35, $1.40 and $1.50, compared with the 34 cents Russians pay.
In an eerie echo of the bickering which derailed Gazprom's first attempt at tapping the international markets two years ago, talk is now of $2.00 per share.
"The price is steadily being talked up all the time. Is the implication of this that if we wait another six months the asking price will go up further?" said the banker.

Lead managers Morgan Stanley and Kleinwort Benson are forced by U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission rules to keep quiet even on the date of the offering, which is already in the public domain, let alone pricing and levels of demand.

What investors are being offered at the roadshows which start in London on October 7 is a dollar denominated security, which avoids direct exposure to the Russian rouble and the settlement and custodianship vagaries of directly owning a Russian share.

In the case of Gazprom, there is an additional incentive as despite being the largest company in Russia, it is one of the most thinly traded on the Moscow bourse as Gazprom imposes restrictions on trading. "We know all of that, yet $1.50 is the absolute top price," said another London-based banker, who declined to be named.
"All of this is extremely sensitive. You just will not be allowed to do business in Russia if you criticise a company which is essentially Russia," he added.
The issue was first mooted two years ago in a deal from Kleinwort Benson but was delayed when the Russian share market collapsed in the wake of the Mexican financial crisis in 1994.

But there was also confusion about how much the company wished to raise and what sort of valuation could be put on it. Gazprom officials, who had planned to sell a nine percent stake, believed that they could get $25 billion for that in 1994, valuing the company in excess of $278 billion, or three times the market capitalisation of U.S. oil major Exxon.
Although price talk started off in a more realistic vein, analysts note that valuations are again becoming stretched.

"Russia's oil and gas industry currently has a market capitalisation of $12 billion. At $2.00 per share, Gazprom would be valued at $46 billion, or around half the market capitalisation of Exxon," said the oil analyst.
The issue was given a further twist on Monday when Russian tax authorities announced that they had frozen its bank accounts to punish it for non-payment of taxes.
Analysts say it is a bizarre move by the authorities on a company which is so closely tied to the centre of power in Russia.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin used to manage Gazprom, while the new energy minister is the former manager of a Gazprom subsidiary.

"There is not other Russian company which is closer to government. Tax is an issue which has been boiling up for years and investors know of the risks of being involved in a new market like Russia and it has not affected sentiment towards Gazprom," said a banker close to the company.
